top.headline: Anthropic launches Claude Ship: agents that fix, review and can approve pull requests
top.why: Claude moves from writing code to being allowed to sign it off, which can remove humans from merges entirely if you enable it. Useful for anyone running a small codebase, but billed separately and uncapped by default.
points: Beta, announced 23-24 Nov: bundles Code Review (generally available) with two new agents, PR Steward and Claude Approvals.
PR Steward fixes failing CI, merge conflicts and review feedback, and comments on each change with how to undo it; it does not approve or merge.
Claude Approvals applies a policy file in the repo; with GitHub auto-merge on, code can merge with no human involved. Anthropic advises starting in observe-only mode.

Team and Enterprise plans, billed on token usage; PR Steward has no spending cap by default. Anthropic says merged PRs on the Claude Code team more than doubled June to September and reverts fell over 40% (company claim). It warns the tool may miss bugs and vulnerabilities.
top.next: Beta now; watch for independent reports of bad auto-merges and any general availability date (none announced in saved articles).

stories.headline: Claude's VP vs VNP proof posted with Lean check but no human verification
stories.why: The earlier claim is now a published paper plus a machine-checked formalisation, yet Anthropic itself says nobody has verified it. It is a test of how science handles AI-authored results.
points: Anthropic's repository credits the paper to Claude alone and claims a superpolynomial lower bound for VP vs VNP over every field; the README says it does not settle P vs NP.
README: both paper and formal proof were written by AI and no human mathematician has checked the proof; Lean checks the proofs but not that the statement says what is claimed.
Reported size varies by outlet (a 70-page paper; roughly 324 Lean files, ~73,000 lines per AI Weekly, not Anthropic).
The Register's framing is critical: the written output is unwieldy rather than explanatory.
stories.next: Human mathematician review of the Lean statements; no date set.

stories.headline: Anthropic opens Enterprise Frontier Safeguards in public beta with zero data retention
stories.why: Sensitive Claude prompts can stay in the customer's own cloud with their keys, removing a common enterprise blocker.
points: Announced 23 Nov for Claude Platform users: prompts, responses and reasoning encrypted and stored in the customer's S3 or Google Cloud.
Anthropic retains nothing and does not train on it; misuse flags go to the customer's security team within a week.
More than 100 customers in the private beta; Bridgewater, Salesforce and Stripe named.
Not available to organisations with HIPAA readiness enabled.
stories.next: Public beta running; general availability not dated.

stories.headline: Ushabti trove at Tanis may point to Sheshonq III's missing tomb
stories.why: A rare case where new finds could settle where a Third Intermediate Period pharaoh was buried, in the era just after the Bible's Shishak-period Egypt. The identification is still an inference, not proven.
points: French team conserving Osorkon II's tomb (r. 872-837 BCE) found 225 ushabti figurines naming Sheshonq III (r. 841-803 BCE).
Found in situ under thick silt in the northern chamber, which had only been partly excavated.
An uninscribed granite sarcophagus found nearby earlier is now thought most likely his; his own tomb has never been located.
Open question: was he buried in his predecessor's tomb, or were his goods moved there? New inscriptions await translation.
stories.next: Translation of the new inscriptions in the northern chamber (no date given).

stories.headline: Eating more egg and peanut in pregnancy did not cut infant allergy in NEJM trial
stories.why: Tests a common idea that a mother's diet can prevent food allergy in high-risk babies. It did not, so the focus stays on feeding allergens to the infant directly.
points: 2,137 pregnant women with a family history of allergy, randomised to at least 6 eggs and 60 peanuts a week or a standard diet (max 3 eggs, 30 peanuts).
Diet followed from before 23 weeks of pregnancy to 4 months of breastfeeding.
Egg or peanut allergy by age 1: 7.8% (83/1,066) versus 8.4% (89/1,064); relative risk 0.93, not significant.
Safety outcomes were similar between groups.
stories.next: None scheduled; watch for guideline bodies' response.
stories.study: Multisite RCT, n=2,137, pregnant women with infants at high allergy risk; outcome at 1 year only, secondhand summary of NEJM paper

stories.headline: Cambridge genome study: about 1 in 5 cancers carry changes matching approved drugs
stories.why: Suggests many patients might qualify for existing drugs if treatment followed DNA rather than tumour site. Benefit in practice is untested.
points: Whole-genome data from over 17,000 tumours: 11,000 primary (UK 100,000 Genomes) and 6,000 metastatic (Dutch Hartwig).
Targetable changes in about 19% of primary and 26% of metastatic cancers.
More than half sat in cancer types where the matching drug lacks FDA approval.
Published in The Lancet Oncology, 16 Nov 2026.
stories.next: Clinical trials of off-label matching would be needed; none dated.
stories.study: Retrospective genomic analysis, >17,000 tumours, UK and Dutch cohorts; no outcome data on treatment benefit; seen via secondary summary

thread.name: Cancer DNA matched to approved drugs

stories.headline: Oestradiol-based menopause hormone therapy linked to better memory, not lower dementia risk
stories.why: Fits the women's-health interest and the tangle of mixed HRT evidence: formulation seems to matter. It is conference data, not trial proof.
points: Analysis of about 14,000 women on different HRT types or none, presented at Neuroscience 2026 (began 14 Nov).
Oestradiol-based therapy tied to better episodic memory than mixed natural/synthetic oestrogens.
In APOE4 carriers, oestradiol users had thicker cortex and less white-matter damage.
HRT did not change progression to dementia; Susan Davis says a randomised trial is needed.
stories.next: Peer-reviewed publication and randomised testing; no date given.

thread.name: Menopause hormone therapy and the brain

stories.study: Observational analysis, ~14,000 women, conference presentation (Neuroscience 2026); not peer-reviewed, cannot show cause
